lessons.title: How Claude Selects Tools — The Role of Descriptions
lessons.summary: Claude never sees a tool's code. It picks a tool only from its name, description and input schema, so the description is the main routing signal. Vague or overlapping descriptions lead to wrong picks.

lessons.title: Writing Tool Descriptions That Route Correctly
lessons.summary: A good description says what the tool does, when to use it, when NOT to use it (and which tool to use instead), what it returns, and what the key parameters mean. Several detailed sentences beat a one-liner.

lessons.title: Designing Tool Input Schemas for Precision and Reliability
lessons.summary: input_schema is JSON Schema. Use specific types, give each property a description with examples or format, keep parameters flat and few, and use clear names (lesson_id, not id).

lessons.title: Required vs. Optional Parameters, Enums, and Constraints
lessons.summary: Mark a parameter required only if the tool cannot run without it; give optional ones sensible defaults. Use enums for a fixed set of values and constraints (min/max, patterns) to narrow valid input. Too many required fields push Claude to invent values.

lessons.title: Strict Tool Use and Valid Inputs
lessons.summary: Setting strict: true on a tool definition guarantees Claude's tool input matches the schema exactly. The schema needs additionalProperties: false, and some keywords (minimum, maximum, minLength) are not supported. Strict checks shape, not business rules, so the tool still validates.

lessons.title: Returning Useful Errors from Tools
lessons.summary: On failure, return is_error: true with an actionable message: what went wrong, why, and how to fix it (for example the list of valid values). Never return raw stack traces or silently empty results. Good errors let Claude correct itself and retry.

lessons.title: Tool Retry Logic and Partial Success Patterns
lessons.summary: Retry only transient failures (timeouts, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff and a cap; never retry permanent ones (400, 404, validation). Make writes idempotent. For batch operations, report per-item success and failure so only the failed items are retried.

lessons.title: Tool Scoping per Agent — Why Less Is More
lessons.summary: Give each agent only the tools its role needs. Fewer tools means more accurate selection, less context used, and a smaller blast radius if something goes wrong.

lessons.title: Selection Heuristics and Tool-Selection Failures
lessons.summary: Common failures: picking a similar but wrong tool, answering from memory instead of calling a tool, calling a tool unnecessarily, and inventing parameter values. Fix them with clearer descriptions, merging or splitting overlapping tools, system-prompt guidance, and evals.

lessons.title: Controlling Tool Selection
lessons.summary: tool_choice controls whether Claude must use tools: auto (Claude decides, the default), any (must use some tool), tool (must use one named tool), none (no tools). disable_parallel_tool_use limits it to one call. Note: the newest models (Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1) reject any/tool, so use auto plus a prompt instruction and strict: true.

lessons.title: Tool Search for Large Catalogs
lessons.summary: With dozens or hundreds of tools, loading every definition wastes context and hurts selection. Mark tools defer_loading: true and add a tool search tool (regex or BM25); Claude searches and only the matching definitions are loaded. At least one tool must stay non-deferred.

lessons.title: What MCP Is and Why It Exists
lessons.summary: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI apps to tools and data. It turns the M x N integration problem into M + N: build a server once and any MCP host can use it. A host (like Claude Desktop) runs one client per server, talking JSON-RPC over stdio (local) or Streamable HTTP (remote).

lessons.title: Tools, Resources, and Prompts — The Three MCP Primitives
lessons.summary: Tools are model-controlled: actions Claude decides to call, which may have side effects. Resources are application-controlled: read-only data identified by a URI that the app chooses to put in context. Prompts are user-controlled: reusable templates with arguments, often shown as slash commands.

lessons.title: Building Your First MCP Server in Python
lessons.summary: Install mcp[cli], create FastMCP("name"), register functions with decorators, and call mcp.run() (stdio by default). Test with the MCP Inspector before writing a client. In a stdio server never print to stdout, because stdout is the protocol channel.

lessons.title: Defining and Exposing Tools via MCP
lessons.summary: @mcp.tool() turns a function into a tool: type hints become the inputSchema and the docstring becomes the description. Use pydantic Field for constraints. Raising an error returns a result with isError. Clients discover tools with tools/list and run them with tools/call.

lessons.title: Defining and Exposing Resources
lessons.summary: @mcp.resource(uri) exposes read-only data. Static resources have a fixed URI; resource templates have {params} like notes://{lesson_id}. Clients discover them with resources/list and resources/templates/list and fetch them with resources/read. The app, not the model, decides what to include.

lessons.title: MCP Prompt Templates — Design and Use Cases
lessons.summary: @mcp.prompt() defines a reusable template that takes arguments and returns a string or a list of messages. Clients list them with prompts/list and fill them with prompts/get. They package proven workflows so users don't have to write good prompts themselves.

lessons.title: Implementing MCP Clients and Connecting to Servers
lessons.summary: A client connects to one server (stdio_client or Streamable HTTP), calls initialize() to negotiate capabilities, then uses list_tools / list_resources / list_prompts and call_tool / read_resource / get_prompt. To use the server with the Claude API, convert each MCP tool (name, description, inputSchema) into a Claude tool (input_schema) and route every tool_use block to session.call_tool.

flashcards.q: What three things does Claude look at to choose a tool?
flashcards.a: The tool's name, description and input schema. It never sees the code.

flashcards.q: Two tools have similar, vague descriptions. What usually happens?
flashcards.a: Claude picks the wrong one inconsistently, because it can't tell them apart.

flashcards.q: Name four things a good tool description includes.
flashcards.a: What it does, when to use it, when NOT to use it (and the alternative), and what it returns.

flashcards.q: Why mention a different tool inside a description?
flashcards.a: To route Claude away from this tool in cases the other tool handles better, e.g. 'For topic search, use search_notes instead.'

flashcards.q: What format is a tool's input_schema written in?
flashcards.a: JSON Schema.

flashcards.q: Why prefer 'lesson_id' over 'id' as a parameter name?
flashcards.a: Specific names remove ambiguity, so Claude fills in the right value.

flashcards.q: When should a parameter be required?
flashcards.a: Only when the tool cannot run without it.

flashcards.q: What does an enum give you over a free-text string?
flashcards.a: Claude can only choose from a fixed set of valid values, so there are no typos or invented options.

flashcards.q: What is the risk of making too many parameters required?
flashcards.a: When Claude lacks the information, it may make up values instead of asking.

flashcards.q: Where do you put strict: true?
flashcards.a: On the tool definition, next to name, description and input_schema (not on tool_choice).

flashcards.q: Name two JSON Schema keywords strict mode does not support.
flashcards.a: Numeric limits like minimum/maximum and string limits like minLength/maxLength.

flashcards.q: Does strict mode remove the need for validation in the tool?
flashcards.a: No. It guarantees the shape of the input, not business rules like 'this lesson exists'.

flashcards.q: Which field marks a tool_result as an error?
flashcards.a: is_error: true

flashcards.q: What makes an error message useful to Claude?
flashcards.a: It says what went wrong, why, and how to fix it, e.g. listing valid values.

flashcards.q: Which errors should you retry and which not?
flashcards.a: Retry transient ones (timeouts, 429, 5xx). Don't retry permanent ones (400, 404, validation errors).

flashcards.q: What should a batch tool return if 8 of 10 items succeed?
flashcards.a: A per-item report, e.g. {imported: 8, failed: [{index, reason}]}, so only the failed items are retried.

flashcards.q: Why should write operations be idempotent when you have retries?
flashcards.a: A retry after a timeout may repeat a write that actually succeeded. Idempotency stops it creating duplicates.

flashcards.q: Give two benefits of giving an agent fewer tools.
flashcards.a: More accurate tool selection and less context used. It also limits the damage if something goes wrong.

flashcards.q: Name three common tool-selection failures.
flashcards.a: Picking a similar but wrong tool, answering from memory instead of calling a tool, and inventing parameter values.

flashcards.q: What are the four tool_choice types?
flashcards.a: auto, any, tool, none.

flashcards.q: On Opus 5.5, how do you get the effect of forcing a tool?
flashcards.a: Forced any/tool returns a 400 there, so use auto, tell Claude in the prompt which tool to use, add strict: true, and check that a tool_use came back.

flashcards.q: Which field hides a tool until tool search finds it?
flashcards.a: defer_loading: true

flashcards.q: What happens if every tool is deferred?
flashcards.a: The API returns a 400. The search tool and at least one other tool must not be deferred.

flashcards.q: What does MCP stand for?
flashcards.a: Model Context Protocol.

flashcards.q: What integration problem does MCP solve?
flashcards.a: M x N: each app needed custom code for each tool. With MCP it's M + N, because a server is built once and works with every host.

flashcards.q: What are the two standard MCP transports?
flashcards.a: stdio for local servers and Streamable HTTP for remote ones.

flashcards.q: Who controls each primitive: tools, resources, prompts?
flashcards.a: Tools: the model. Resources: the application. Prompts: the user.

flashcards.q: Can a resource have side effects?
flashcards.a: No. Resources are read-only data. Actions with side effects belong in tools.

flashcards.q: Which transport does mcp.run() use by default?
flashcards.a: stdio.

flashcards.q: Why must a stdio MCP server never print() to stdout?
flashcards.a: stdout carries the JSON-RPC messages, so extra output corrupts the protocol. Log to stderr instead.

flashcards.q: In FastMCP, what becomes the tool's description?
flashcards.a: The function's docstring.

flashcards.q: What are the MCP method names for discovering and running tools?
flashcards.a: tools/list and tools/call.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a resource and a resource template?
flashcards.a: A resource has a fixed URI (course://syllabus). A template has parameters (notes://{lesson_id}).

flashcards.q: Which MCP method reads a resource's content?
flashcards.a: resources/read

flashcards.q: How are MCP prompts usually shown to users?
flashcards.a: As slash commands or menu items the user picks.

flashcards.q: Which MCP methods list prompts and fill one with arguments?
flashcards.a: prompts/list and prompts/get.

flashcards.q: What must a client call right after connecting?
flashcards.a: initialize(), which negotiates the protocol version and capabilities.

flashcards.q: Which field name differs between an MCP tool and a Claude API tool?
flashcards.a: MCP uses inputSchema; the Claude API uses input_schema. name and description map directly.
